column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about Operation Midnight Hammer: the American air strike on three nuclear sites in Iran, on the night of the twenty-first to the twenty-second of June 2025. The bombers flew from Missouri and back, using some of the largest conventional bombs in the American arsenal, against a site built inside a mountain. Reaching the targets was one question. What the bombs destroyed, and what the strike changed, are others, and they are still argued about. We will tell you what is known, who says what, and what is still not known.

Operation midnight hammer. In the early hours of the twenty-second of June 2025, Iranian time, American B two bombers struck Iran's uranium enrichment sites at for-doe and na-tanz. A submarine fired cruise missiles at a third site, at is-fa-hahn. It happened during a war between Israel and Iran, which had begun nine days earlier. The bombers returned home safely. The United States called the strike a success. International inspectors could not see what had happened underground, and estimates of the damage differed. The next day Iran fired missiles at an American base in Qatar. Hours later, a ceasefire between Israel and Iran was announced.

Enrichment is not a bomb. Enrichment raises the share of uranium two thirty-five. Most nuclear power reactors use uranium enriched to much lower levels. Enriched uranium is a material. A nuclear weapon is a separate device. for-doe and na-tanz were uranium enrichment plants. The United States used conventional bombs in this operation.

Who is who. Iran: the Supreme Leader, Ali ha-meh-nay; the President, Masoud peh-zesh-kee-ahn; the Foreign Minister, Abbas a-rag-chee. The United States: President Donald Trump; Defence Secretary Pete heg-seth; General Dan cane, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; and General Erik koo-ril-a, who commanded American forces in the Middle East. On this page Iran is red and the United States is blue. The International Atomic Energy Agency, or I A E A, inspects nuclear sites and reports what it can verify. Rafael gross-ee was its director general.

How this page tells it. Each line is tagged with where it comes from. What a government says is that government's claim. The flights are drawn as simple arrows. The real routes were secret, and are not known in detail. This page shows no one hurt, and does not show how the bombs worked underground. The story ends with the ceasefire of June 2025. A short note at the end says what was still unknown in November 2026.

Three sites. for-doe lies in the hills north-east of the city of kome. Its enrichment halls were built deep inside a mountain, to protect them from attack. na-tanz, further south, was Iran's main enrichment site, with halls above and below ground. is-fa-hahn held a nuclear technology centre, where uranium was converted and processed.

A long dispute. In 2015, Iran agreed with world powers to limit its nuclear programme and accept close inspection. In 2018 the United States left the agreement and renewed its sanctions. In 2019, Iran began exceeding the deal's limits. The I A E A estimated that, by the seventeenth of May 2025, Iran held just over four hundred kilograms of uranium enriched up to sixty percent. Iran said its nuclear programme was for peaceful purposes. In March 2025, American intelligence assessed that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon, and that its leader had not restarted the weapons programme stopped in 2003. It added that pressure on him to do so had probably grown.

The twelfth of June. On the twelfth of June 2025, the agency's board found that Iran had breached its safeguards obligations by failing to cooperate fully and promptly with inspectors investigating undeclared nuclear material and activities. Reuters reported that nineteen countries voted for the finding, three against, and eleven abstained, in a closed-door vote. It was the first such finding against Iran in about twenty years. The finding was not a discovery of a bomb. Iran rejected it.

The thirteenth of June. On the thirteenth of June, Israel attacked Iran's nuclear sites and military leaders. Iran answered with missiles fired at Israel. na-tanz and is-fa-hahn were struck by Israel in the first days of the war. Any picture of them after the twenty-second may show damage from both attacks. The United States and Iran had been holding talks, through Oman. The next round, set for the fifteenth of June, was called off.

Whiteman. Early on the twenty-first of June, seven B two stealth bombers took off from Whiteman Air Force Base, in Missouri, and flew east. At the same time, other B twos flew west, over the Pacific Ocean. They were a decoy, to draw attention away from the real mission. Each B two has a crew of two. General cane said very few people in Washington knew the timing or nature of the plan.

Across the world. The bombers flew for about eighteen hours to reach Iran, refuelling in the air from tanker aircraft several times. The bombers were supported by fighter jets and air-refuelling tankers. The Pentagon said more than one hundred and twenty-five American aircraft took part. On this map, the route is simplified. The real route was not published.

for-doe, ten past two. At about ten past two in the morning in Iran, which was twenty to seven in the evening in Washington, the first B two released its bombs over for-doe. They were G B U fifty-sevens, called Massive Ordnance Penetrators, each weighing about thirty thousand pounds. It was the first time the United States had used these conventional bombs in combat. General cane later described about fifteen years of work on the problem by two officers of an American defence agency.

na-tanz and is-fa-hahn. na-tanz was struck too. The Pentagon reported that fourteen of these bombs were used across for-doe and na-tanz. An American submarine fired more than two dozen Tomahawk cruise missiles at is-fa-hahn. The Pentagon said they were the last weapons to strike. All three sites were struck within twenty-five minutes. In all, the United States used about seventy-five precision weapons.

The way home. General cane said Iran's fighters did not fly, and that its air defences appeared not to have seen the bombers. He said the Pentagon was unaware of any shots fired at the strike force as it left Iranian airspace. The bombers flew home to Missouri. The whole mission lasted about a day and a half. The Pentagon called it the second-longest B two mission ever flown. No American aircraft was reported lost.

Obliterated. That evening, President Trump announced the strike. He said Iran's key nuclear enrichment facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated". The next morning, General cane said the Pentagon's initial assessment pointed to severe damage at all three sites, and that the final assessment would take time. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas a-rag-chee, called the attack "outrageous", and said it would have "everlasting consequences".

What the inspectors could see. On the twenty-third of June, the I A E A's director general, Rafael gross-ee, said craters could be seen at for-doe. gross-ee expected very significant damage, but said the extent of the damage underground could not yet be assessed. Iran told the I A E A there was no rise in radiation outside the three sites.

Months, or years?. News reports on the twenty-fourth of June described a leaked preliminary assessment by the Defence Intelligence Agency. It estimated a setback of months. American officials described the assessment as low confidence. On the second of July, the Pentagon said the programme had been set back by one to two years. It did not publish its evidence. In September, the I A E A reported that it lacked access to verify Iran's highly enriched uranium inventory. The two American assessments gave different estimates of the setback. The I A E A reported a separate problem: it could not verify the highly enriched uranium inventory.

al oo-dayd. On the twenty-third of June, Iran fired missiles at al oo-dayd, a Qatari air base that hosts American forces. Reuters reported that Iran gave advance notice. A Qatari military officer said one of nineteen missiles hit the base. Qatar reported no casualties.

Ceasefire. Hours after the attack on al oo-dayd, President Trump announced a ceasefire between Israel and Iran. The ceasefire followed soon afterward. The timing alone cannot tell us how much the strike contributed. The ceasefire took effect on the twenty-fourth of June, after twelve days of war.

Questions in Washington. President Trump told Congress the strikes were "limited in scope and purpose", in the "collective self-defense" of Israel, under his own authority as commander in chief. Some members of Congress argued that he needed their approval first. On the twenty-seventh of June, a motion to bring the war-powers resolution out of committee failed in the Senate, with forty-seven votes in favour and fifty-three against. Washington defended the strike as necessary and lawful. Iran condemned it as illegal. Its legality is still debated.

What is not known. What exactly was destroyed inside for-doe is not publicly known. The I A E A had yet to verify the whereabouts and condition of the full stockpile of enriched uranium. The sources used for this page do not establish whether anyone was killed at the three sites in the American strikes.

After June 2025. In November 2026, Reuters reported that the I A E A was still seeking access to the bombed sites and an accounting of the enriched uranium. A new war began on the twenty-eighth of February 2026. On the third of March, the I A E A said satellite images showed fresh damage to entrance buildings at na-tanz. Later images need to be dated carefully, because they can show damage from more than one attack. That war is not told on this page. The bombers reached their targets and came home. What the strike achieved is still argued about. History asks what happened, what was claimed, and how we know.
